default: You take the east road again. At the checkpoint you tell your story, and they let you through. Then Harrow, and the edge of the forest.

default.text: The ruins take you back as a place does that has not changed while you have. There is the grey light, and the heavy silence, and the Watcher at the gate just as before, who says "[player]" again as you pass, in the same flat voice.
default.else: The ruins take you back as a place does that has not changed while you have. There is the grey light, and the heavy silence, and the Watcher at the gate just as before, who does not turn.

default.text: They are turning the bone figure over and over in their hands.

default: [missing person] is where you left them. They look up when they hear you coming through the outskirts. They have spent months listening for footsteps, and they knew yours before they looked.
text.commander:
You sit down across from them in the outskirts and tell them about Crestfall as you would report to a fellow officer: where the Compact stands, Seriva, Vorne's daughter, the fragment, and Pol.

They listen with their whole attention. When you have finished they say, "Time is running out."

"Yes," you say.

"Then we spend two days making sure we do it properly," they say. "Not quickly. Properly."
text.arcane:
You tell them what Pol told you: that the Covenant's purification and the old sealing are two different rituals, and what each of them is, and what each of them costs.

They are quiet for a moment. "I knew there was another ritual," they say. "The chamber walls speak of it. A second way, which they call the lesser way, because it does not need the same bond between the two people." They pause. "The Covenant's ritual will work. It will stop the curse. And it will be a catastrophe."

"Yes," you say.

"Then we do the right one," they say.
text.ranger:
You tell them briskly, and they ask the right questions: how strong the Compact is, where Seriva is, the fragment, and whether Pol is ready.

Then they ask, "How are you?"

It catches you out. You have been on the move, weighing things up and managing them, ever since you left the ruins. The question is so simple, the one people ask each other and mean, that it seems to come from another life.

"Getting by," you say.

They very nearly smile. "That is what I thought you would say. Rest tonight. We begin tomorrow."
text.cipher:
You give them the whole picture, in the order that makes most sense: the dangers, how long you have, what you have to work with, and what may go wrong.

They listen, and then they say, "You have not told me how any of it made you feel."

"That's not what matters," you say.

They look at you a long while. "For the ritual," they say, "it is all that matters. The mechanism reads what is real. Not what you show it. What you really carry."

They pause. "So. How are you?"

choices.text: Begin getting ready for the ritual. Two days, done properly.

default.text:
They take you back into the inner approach, though not to the chamber yet. They show you the parts of the carving that concern the two people: what the ritual will ask of you, and what you will need to be ready for.

So the work of the next two days begins.

choices.text: Spend the evening talking. Not about the ritual, only talking.

default.text:
The Watcher sits at the gate, and the ruins lie all round you. The grey light fades towards whatever does duty for night here.

You talk. You don't talk about the ritual, or Crestfall, or what happens next. You talk about before, about what life was like before either of you came to Ashenveld, about the things that made you, and about what has been between you all through eleven years and a hundred miles and fourteen months of silence.

By the time the light has quite gone you understand something about what the mechanism reads. It doesn't read what you show it. It reads what you really carry.

And you understand why it needed two people who knew each other this well.

text.default:
You spend two days in the outskirts of the ruins.

[missing person] teaches you the shape of the ritual patiently. They have eight months of learning to pass on in two days. They are a good teacher, or they have become one, here, with nobody to teach.

The ritual has three parts. There is the approach, which is what you do before you go into the chamber, and how you make ready what is between you for the mechanism to read. There is the engagement, which is what happens in the chamber: where each of you stands, what you must do, and the moment when you touch. And there is the sealing, which is what happens if the mechanism answers as it should. The text describes it, but they admit they don't wholly understand it.

"The builders were honest that they did not wholly understand what they were doing," they say. "They knew it worked. They did not know exactly why."
text.commander:
You treat the two days as training. You know what you have to do, the method is as well set down as anything you are likely to get, and you know the risks. So you prepare.

On the evening of the second day they ask whether you are ready.

"I've done harder things with less preparation," you say.

"That is not what I asked," they say.

"I'm ready," you say, and you mean it.
text.arcane:
They are two days of the hardest study you have ever done.

The ritual is a beautiful piece of work. It uses the mechanism's own purpose to seal it again, instead of forcing it, as the Covenant's ritual would. It asks the mechanism to remember what it is and do it once more, and the two people are both the asking and the showing.

By the end of the first day you understand it in principle. The second day is given to practice, which needs a very different kind of preparation.
text.ranger:
They show you what to do, and you learn it by doing it. The movements of the ritual are exact: certain places, and certain actions at certain moments. You learn them as you learn ground, by going over it until it is in your body and not only in your head.

On the second evening they sit down across from you and say, "The ritual needs you to mean it. Everything you do in that chamber must be truly meant. The mechanism reads what you intend, not what you perform."

"I know," you say. You have been meaning things all your life. It is the one thing that needs no practice.
text.cipher:
You have never got ready for anything in quite this way before.

The ritual doesn't ask you to be skilful, or brave, or clever. It asks you to be there: to be exactly who you are, with the person you are with, at this point in both your lives.

You have spent a long time being exactly who you are not. Getting ready for this ritual is, in a way, a matter of putting down something you have carried for years.

success.text:
You are as ready as two days of teaching can make you. [missing person] looks at you on the evening of the second day. They have given you everything they know, and now they wait to see what you will do with it.

"Tomorrow," they say.

"Tomorrow," you say.

You both sleep in the outskirts, in the camp they have made, under the grey of the deep forest where no sky shows. You sleep better than you have since you came to Ashenveld.

success_at_cost.text:
You are ready, though not altogether. There are parts of the ritual that have not quite settled, ideas that stay a little out of reach. [missing person] says, "It is enough. The mechanism does not need you to be perfect. It needs you to be honest."

You take them at their word.

failure.text:
It hasn't taken properly. You can feel it, as you can feel it when you have learned the words of something and not the sense. [missing person] can see it too.

"We need another day," they say. "Going in before you are ready is worse than taking the extra time."

choices.text: You're worn out. Rest, and let [missing person] go over it alone.

default.text:
You sleep through most of the second day. When you wake they are sitting by the fire with the chamber text spread over their knees, mouthing the words.

"You will know enough," they say, without looking up. You are not sure either of you believes it.

text.default:
Pol comes to the outskirts of the ruins on the evening before the ritual.

She comes alone and on foot, over the edge of the forest without any trouble. She has plainly been here before; she knows the path and the safe ways through the outskirts. She has the fragment wrapped in a cloth, and a pack of the herbs Maret's camp uses against long exposure.

She greets [missing person] as though she had been expecting them for years.

Then she finds you. "Maret sent word," she says. "The Compact has been asking questions about the east road, and Seriva has been seen with a map. You have less time than we thought."
text.commander:
There is less time than you thought. You go over it. Seriva has a map, she knows roughly where to look, and she is on the move. The checkpoint is manned, but you got past it, and a Covenant scholar with the Compact behind her could get past it too, or simply go round it.

"How long?" you ask Pol.

"Days," she says. "Not weeks. Two days, perhaps. Perhaps less."
text.arcane:
Seriva has a map of the country from twenty years ago. The outskirts have changed since then; you know it from walking through them. The paths have shifted, and the curse lies thick in different places. But the inner approach will be where it always was.

If she has her map from that first visit, she can find the inner approach. It will take her a while, but she can find it.
text.ranger:
Two days, perhaps less. You set that against what the ritual needs.

The ritual takes about three hours in the chamber, from the approach to the sealing. Pol will be outside, and you and [missing person] inside.

If Seriva reaches the outskirts before it is finished, she will find Pol. Pol is one old woman, and Seriva will have the Compact with her.

You don't much like the sum.
text.cipher:
The news changes things, and you work it out again.

The ritual must be tomorrow, not the day after. You have done what preparation you have done. Going in not quite ready is now less of a risk than waiting.

You look at [missing person]. They have come to the same conclusion; you can see it in their face.

choices.text: The ritual is tomorrow. Whatever time you have, you have.

default.text:
"Tomorrow," you say.

[missing person] nods, and Pol nods. It is decided.

You do not spend the evening going over the ritual again. That is done. You spend it with the people who are here because of you, and because of choices each of you made: Pol with her fifteen years of waiting, [missing person] with their fourteen months, and you with eleven years before all this and the few days since.

The fire is small, and the ruins are quiet round you. The Watcher sits at the gate.

choices.text: Send word to Maret, and ask her to hold Seriva up if she can.

text: Pol can take a message back to the camp before she comes to witness the ritual. You write something short. There are things at the Rootless camp that Seriva will need, and she will have to get them through Vorne; and Vorne's daughter is at the camp; and Maret can make getting them difficult enough to cost Seriva a day.
Pol takes the message and goes. She will be back before morning.
You may have bought another day. You may not need it, or it may make all the difference.

text.text: The message goes to Edric as well. He locks the shrine's map room, and Seriva loses a day finding another copy.

success_at_cost.text: The message goes, but you are not confident it will work. Maret has little hold over Seriva, even through Vorne. It may buy a few hours, not a day.

failure.text: The message goes, but you don't believe it will make much difference. Seriva is not easily held up. You go on without counting on the extra time.

choices.text: Pay one of the camp's runners to take word to Maret.

text: You count eight coins into Pol's hand for the boy who runs the camp's messages, and write something short. There are things at the Rootless camp that Seriva will need, and she will have to get them through Vorne; and Vorne's daughter is at the camp; and Maret can make getting them difficult enough to cost Seriva a day.
Pol goes back to the forest edge to send the boy off. She will be back before morning.
You may have bought another day. You may not need it, or it may make all the difference.

text.text: The message goes to Edric as well. He locks the shrine's map room, and Seriva loses a day finding another copy.

text.default:
It is late. Pol is asleep and the fire has burned low. You and [missing person] are the last ones awake.

It was bound to happen. You both have things to say, and you have each been waiting for the right moment, and now there is no time left to wait for it.

They speak first.

"The ritual will read everything," they say. "I need you to know that before we go in. Not only what you want for the sealing. Everything. What you feel about me. What you are afraid of. What you have been carrying since before you came here."

They pause. "The mechanism does not judge. It only reads. But you should know that I will see it. All of you."

The fire cracks. The ruins are dark beyond the circle of its warmth.
text.commander:
You have spent a whole career managing what other people see of you. You have done it so long that it has become your nature.

"And you?" you say. "It'll read you too."

"Yes," they say.

"Then we go in even," you say. It is either a frightening thought, or the most honest thing you have said in years. Very likely it is both.
text.arcane:
You think about everything the mechanism will read: the ambition, the hunger to know things, and eleven years in a library because everywhere else hurt.

"I understand," you say.

"Do you mind?" they ask.

You think about it honestly. "No," you say. "I mind that you'll see it. I don't mind the mechanism seeing it."

They look at you. "Why the difference?"

"Because I know what the mechanism will do with what it sees," you say. "I'm less sure about you."
text.ranger:
You have spent years being exactly what was needed and no more, quick and plain and easy to read.

But this is different. The mechanism doesn't want quick. It wants the truth.

"I came here for you," you say. "Not for Ashenveld. Not because I knew what was in the ruins. I came because of you." You stop for a moment. "Whatever else it reads, that'll be the plainest thing in it."
text.cipher:
You have spent your life reading other people, and being read less than you wanted to be. The thought of something that reads you entirely, not in part and not just what you choose to show, is either the most comforting thought you have had in years or the least.

You have not decided which.

"I'm going to tell you something I've never told anyone," you say.

And you do.

choices.text: Tell them everything you're carrying, before the mechanism does.

text: You talk for an hour. The fire goes out, and neither of you gets up to build it again. You go on talking in the dark.

text.text: "I said I'd write," you say. "I wrote twice. I haven't got a reason. I've been looking for one for eleven years."
"I never told you it was over," you say. "I just went. I think I wanted it to stay not over."
"I left you with the house," you say. "And with her, at the end. I knew what I was leaving you with, and I went anyway."
"You told me to go," you say. "I thought you were tired of me. I let myself think it for eleven years because it was easier than asking."
"We never finished that argument," you say. "I've had it with you every night for eleven years. You win most of them."
"I left before I had to say it," you say. "So I'm saying it now, in the dark, where I can't see your face."

text: When you have finished, they are quiet a long while.
Then they say, "Thank you. For not making me find out in the chamber."
You sleep. In the morning you go to the chamber.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let the mechanism read what it reads.

default.text:
You keep quiet. They understand, or at any rate they accept it, which is nearly the same.

"All right," they say. "The mechanism will know."

"Yes," you say. "I know."

You sleep, and in the morning you go to the chamber.

But the silence between you is not quite what it was. It is no worse. It is only that now you both know it is there.
